Gift Ngoepe

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...the first African to play major league baseball.

Unique Selling Point:
A Story about a South African who has made history by becoming the first person ever from Africa to play major league baseball.

Summary:
A Pittsburgh Pirates rookie named Gift Ngoepe, who grew up in Johannesburg, South Africa, has become the first African-born player to appear in a Major League Baseball game.

Further information:
In the wee hours on the morning of Freedom Day, April 27, a South African made Major League Baseball (MLB) history.

In a moment that most South Africans would not have been aware of at the time, Mpho "Gift" Ngoepe, 27, made his MLB debut, playing second base when he ran on in the fourth innings for the Pittsburgh Pirates.

After an eight-and-a-half-year wait since signing with the 'Bucs' back in 2008, Ngoepe finally pulled on his No 61 jersey in the big leagues as the world looked on.

Raised in Randburg, there weren't too many places where a boy could fall in love with baseball, but growing up in a ballpark clubhouse was the best possible start.

Ngoepe along with his mother, Maureen, and younger brother, Victor, resided in a tiny room attached to the clubhouse of the Randburg Mets - one of only a couple Gauteng baseball clubs - where Maureen worked as an attendant.

It was that connection to baseball that saw Ngoepe fall in love with the sport and so began his journey to fulfil a dream of playing in the big leagues, just like his Hall of Fame icon, Barry Larkin.

"It was a little difficult to get sponsors to take us on trips so we could get more exposure while we were youngsters," Ngoepe told Sport24.

"It was really hard. We had to compete against three other sports (rugby, soccer and cricket) and baseball could not grow in the youth department ... it became difficult to get better competition."

In 2008, Ngoepe was invited to a MLB academy in Italy where he was spotted by a Pirates scout.

Just like that, Ngoepe had his big break and he became the first black South African to sign a professional baseball contract. He was 18-years-old.

He represented South Africa at the 2009 World Baseball Classic where he impressed by hitting consecutive triples off Mexico's Elmer Dessens in a 14-3 loss.


Based in America and still struggling to make it to the top, Ngoepe's journey was rocked by tragedy when his mother was diagnosed with double pneumonia and passed away in 2013.

Ngoepe, who returned to South Africa immediately after hearing the news, had to take guardianship of his then 15-year-old brother, Victor.

Victor accompanied his older brother back to the United States, where he is currently also pursuing a career in baseball.

Losing his mother left Ngoepe more determined than ever to put in the hard yards, and he worked his way through the system.

Last week Wednesday at PNC Park against the reigning MLB champions, the Chicago Cubs, when Ngoepe finally made his debut on a day that not only meant a lot to him, but also to many South Africans, he had spent nine seasons in the minors.

It was fitting for Ngoepe that his debut came on a day that is so significant for South Africans.

"South Africa has come a long way as a country," he said.

"I know we still battle with racial issues, but we've come a long way with Freedom Day and everything that has happened and knowing that Nelson Mandela opened doors for people and united us as a country.

"To have it (my debut) on that day ... it couldn’t be scripted any better than that."

Having walked out in front of a packed Pittsburgh crowd, Ngoepe stepped up to the plate in the bottom of the fourth and recorded a single up the middle off Cubs pitcher Jon Lester in the first at-bat of his career.

Ngoepe finished his whirlwind debut with a single in the fourth, a walk in the sixth and was struck out in the eighth as the Pirates clinched a 6-5 victory over the Cubs.

Despite baseball not being popular in the country, Ngoepe's debut made its rounds in social media as South Africans took pride in one of their own making it on the biggest stage.

Ngoepe was delighted with the recognition he and the game fought so hard for received from back home.

"It feels great that they are acknowledging baseball - it's a great sport," said Ngoepe.

"I decided to pursue it as a dream from a very young age and I hope it grows in South Africa."

Now as a professional Major League Baseball player, Ngoepe won't have much time to visit, but he emphasised that the country will always remain close to his heart as he often misses having a braai with his family and friends.

After tasting the sweet success of the Majors, Ngoepe is not going to give up on his ultimate dream.

"My goal is to stay in the big leagues, as long as I can and hopefully I can retire and they can retire my number as well," he said.

Press Release:


In South Africa, baseball is a little known sport, but for Gift Ngoepe it’s the game that has catapulted him into international stardom. From playing on the streets of
Randburg to competing in Major League Baseball in the US, Ngoepe has reached the pinnacle of professional baseball becoming the first player from Africa to reach this
level in the sport. Carte Blanche visits Ngoepe behind the scenes at the home base of the Pittsburgh Pirates

Script:


V/O:
Professional baseball in the US is huge. It is the biggest spectator sport in the country and is played in massive stadiums, attracting millions of fans.

Every big-league game is broadcast worldwide and last year Major League Baseball generated 130 billion rands worth of revenue.

Merchandising is also massive, from clothing to baseball cards that collectors pay millions for.

Franchises have teams at different levels, from rookie up through the minor leagues; to what is known as the big leagues where only the best of the best compete.

At this level players are superstars, and earn massive amounts of money. For example, this is Clayton Kershaw of the LA Dodgers. This year his salary is a staggering 470 million rand. The lowest paid players at this level earn a cool 7 million rands a year.

It is incredibly difficult to reach the top. Only 30 of every 100 000 high school baseball players ever make it to the big leagues and for foreign-based player to make it, the odds are 1 in several million.

But this year a South African defeated the odds and became the first African born player to play major league baseball. His name is Gift Ngoepe and his debut was on the 26th of April.

UPSOUND Commentator:

...at 2:45 South African time, Gift Ngoepe has made history.

It is so difficult to reach the top because so much skill is required in the sport.


Gift:
This game is not the easiest of games to play. I mean, you are going to fail sever out the 10 times that you play the sport. They give you a round ball and an round bat and then they say square this ball up. And it’s like a game of inches, if you miss the ball by this much, you have missed it.
V/O:
Gift’s team is The Pittsburgh Pirates’ and their home ground is the massive PNC Park. It is there we caught up with Gift just before a game. He is a midfielder and very comfortable with the other major league superstars. Gift has come a long way, a very long way to be here. It all started at this baseball club in Randburg. 18
LINK:
The Randburg Mets Club has a special place in Gift Ngoepe’s remarkable story. In fact, he grew up here. In a room in this very clubhouse.
Gift:
It all started with my mom working at Randburg Mets baseball club and I was with my grandparents in Limpopo where I was born and my mom was working at Randburg Mets and I happen to be sick and my grandmother could not look after me, so she called my mom to come and get me.
V/O:
Maureen worked at the club as a cleaner. She also lived on the premises in a small room attached to the clubhouse. That is where Gift grew up. His older brother Christopher lived and went to school in Limpopo. Maureen later had another son, Victor, who lived with her and Gift at the clubhouse.

Sadly, Maureen passed away in 2013. At the club, we met Christopher, who is enthusiastic about his younger brother’s achievements.
32
Christopher:
I think it’s a good thing for him. Playing major leagues was his dream. It’s a goal he wanted to reach. And that’s a promise he made to our mother before she passed away. That this is what he wanted to achieve. Even though there was a point in time when he wanted to quit. Maybe he thought he couldn’t get that far. But I encouraged him and told him “Please continue to play baseball because that is what you do best.” So, I’m very happy to see him playing there, having achieved the dream he had for a long time.
V/O:
Christopher now lives in the very same room his younger brothers shared with their mother. It is tiny, but it was home.
12
Gift:
There was not much room at all. It was a small room that was able to give us comfort and give us a roof over our head and my mom was able to put food on the table and it was a fun household for me. Just being able to eat as a family, watch TV as a family, and have good and bad times together as a family in this one little unit that we had.
LINK:
The Randburg Mets is an active club that plays in a Johannesburg-wide league and living at the clubhouse Gift got to see baseball virtually every day.
10
Gift:
And I saw people play with this bat and ball and thye had a glove on and it intrigued me a little bit and I am like ”This seems fun”. So I started practicing by myself on the side.
V/O:
Paul Kindt is an experienced baseball coach who encountered Gift at the club.
5
Coach:
I came to Randburg and I saw this little young guy running around the field with a glove that was three time to big for him. But tremendous skills. You could just see then at the age of 7 or 8, that Gift was going ot go somewhere. He had the talent.
Gift:
One day they had practice and I was throwing the ball against the wall and the coach shouted for me and he was “Hey, why doen’t you come and join us?” and that is how it all started for me.
Paul:
Gift grew up at the club. So he got to know all the guys, the senior players, and they would play with him. So they taught him how to catch, how to throw, how to hit the ball, how to play the game. So Gift at a very young age was taught by some of the best players in the province. How to play the game and how to do things right. He wouldshow the skills of being a wonderful, wonderful athlete.
V/O:
Gift’s exceptional talent showed from early on and as he grew older he played for a variety of club teams and won many awards for outstanding performances. He represented South Africa at both junior and senior levels. In time word of his talent reached the United States.
17
Gift:
In 2007 I was invited to the MLB Academy in Italy.
V/O:
Major League Baseball holds these academies to develop baseball around the world and also to find new talent. The next year Gift was invited back to the academy and at the end of 30 days training, the Pittsburgh Pirates offered him a rookie contract. He started to play in the lower or minor leagues in 2009. And this year after 9 years in the minor leagues he finally made it right to the top. He became one of the elite 25-man roster, the best of the best. On his debut, his fellow teammates laughingly checked his heartbeat.
34
Gift:
It is quite an experience and it is an overwhelming atmosphere to be in. There is nothing like it that you go through. I mean, I know being at a soccer stadium and Kaiser Chiefs vs Orlando Pirates and me blowing the Vuvuzela. But being at the field and seeing all of this in can be very overwhelming. It is scary at times when there are so many people watching you.
V/O:
After Maureen died in 2013, Gift took his younger brother Victor who is also a talented baseball player, with him to the US. It paid off and this year Victor started to play for the Pirates at the rookie level. Christopher thinks he will also make it to the top.
13
Christopher:
Yes, I think he is the type of man... the type of boy who enjoys baseball. And he is also somebody who has a passion for it. So that’s why he followed in the footsteps of his brother. I think the two of them really have a passion for the sport. That’s why you see them both playing in America. I am really happy that they are playing baseball in America.
V/O:
Back here at the club where he grew up, Gifts exploits are also celebrated. Coenraad van Rensburg currently plays for the Mets.
Coenraad:
He is an amazing man who always has a smile on his face. That big smile you see on TV. He is very generous and passionate about the sport. In his off-time when he comes here in the off-season, November December you will find him on the field. He will be playing baseball, soccer with his brother Victor, he’s be helping the kids, the little leagues throw a ball better, at a ball better. He still lives here when he is here. This is is home. I think this is where his heart is.
V/O:
For Gift making it to where he is now, is a dream come true, but it was not always easy.
Gift:
It took a lot of hard work and determination and it took a lot of people to be believe in me and me to believe in myself.
9
V/O:
And if Gift’s long journey taught him one thing, it is this:
Gift:
Dreams can come true.

He will be playing baseball, soccer with his brother Victor, he’s be helping the kids, the little leagues throw a ball better, at a ball better. He still lives here when he is here. This is is home. I think this is where his heart is. V/O: For Gift making it to where he is now, is a dream come true, but it was not always easy. Gift: It took a lot of hard work and determination and it took a lot of people to be believe in me and me to believe in myself. 9 V/O: And if Gift’s long journey taught him one thing, it is this: Gift: Dreams can come true.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ...the first African to play major league baseball.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A Story about a South African who has made history by becoming the first person ever from Africa to play major league baseball.
metadata.Summary: A Pittsburgh Pirates rookie named Gift Ngoepe, who grew up in Johannesburg, South Africa, has become the first African-born player to appear in a Major League Baseball game.
metadata.Further information: In the wee hours on the morning of Freedom Day, April 27, a South African made Major League Baseball (MLB) history. In a moment that most South Africans would not have been aware of at the time, Mpho "Gift" Ngoepe, 27, made his MLB debut, playing second base when he ran on in the fourth innings for the Pittsburgh Pirates. After an eight-and-a-half-year wait since signing with the 'Bucs' back in 2008, Ngoepe finally pulled on his No 61 jersey in the big leagues as the world looked on. Raised in Randburg, there weren't too many places where a boy could fall in love with baseball, but growing up in a ballpark clubhouse was the best possible start. Ngoepe along with his mother, Maureen, and younger brother, Victor, resided in a tiny room attached to the clubhouse of the Randburg Mets - one of only a couple Gauteng baseball clubs - where Maureen worked as an attendant. It was that connection to baseball that saw Ngoepe fall in love with the sport and so began his journey to fulfil a dream of playing in the big leagues, just like his Hall of Fame icon, Barry Larkin. "It was a little difficult to get sponsors to take us on trips so we could get more exposure while we were youngsters," Ngoepe told Sport24. "It was really hard. We had to compete against three other sports (rugby, soccer and cricket) and baseball could not grow in the youth department ... it became difficult to get better competition." In 2008, Ngoepe was invited to a MLB academy in Italy where he was spotted by a Pirates scout. Just like that, Ngoepe had his big break and he became the first black South African to sign a professional baseball contract. He was 18-years-old. He represented South Africa at the 2009 World Baseball Classic where he impressed by hitting consecutive triples off Mexico's Elmer Dessens in a 14-3 loss. Based in America and still struggling to make it to the top, Ngoepe's journey was rocked by tragedy when his mother was diagnosed with double pneumonia and passed away in 2013. Ngoepe, who returned to South Africa immediately after hearing the news, had to take guardianship of his then 15-year-old brother, Victor. Victor accompanied his older brother back to the United States, where he is currently also pursuing a career in baseball. Losing his mother left Ngoepe more determined than ever to put in the hard yards, and he worked his way through the system. Last week Wednesday at PNC Park against the reigning MLB champions, the Chicago Cubs, when Ngoepe finally made his debut on a day that not only meant a lot to him, but also to many South Africans, he had spent nine seasons in the minors. It was fitting for Ngoepe that his debut came on a day that is so significant for South Africans. "South Africa has come a long way as a country," he said. "I know we still battle with racial issues, but we've come a long way with Freedom Day and everything that has happened and knowing that Nelson Mandela opened doors for people and united us as a country. "To have it (my debut) on that day ... it couldn’t be scripted any better than that." Having walked out in front of a packed Pittsburgh crowd, Ngoepe stepped up to the plate in the bottom of the fourth and recorded a single up the middle off Cubs pitcher Jon Lester in the first at-bat of his career. Ngoepe finished his whirlwind debut with a single in the fourth, a walk in the sixth and was struck out in the eighth as the Pirates clinched a 6-5 victory over the Cubs. Despite baseball not being popular in the country, Ngoepe's debut made its rounds in social media as South Africans took pride in one of their own making it on the biggest stage. Ngoepe was delighted with the recognition he and the game fought so hard for received from back home. "It feels great that they are acknowledging baseball - it's a great sport," said Ngoepe. "I decided to pursue it as a dream from a very young age and I hope it grows in South Africa." Now as a professional Major League Baseball player, Ngoepe won't have much time to visit, but he emphasised that the country will always remain close to his heart as he often misses having a braai with his family and friends. After tasting the sweet success of the Majors, Ngoepe is not going to give up on his ultimate dream. "My goal is to stay in the big leagues, as long as I can and hopefully I can retire and they can retire my number as well," he said.
